# How to use this guide

Environmental Sciences is a descriptive, scoring subject with no numericals. Marks come from neat definitions, classifications, labelled flow diagrams (food chain, energy pyramid, nitrogen cycle, sewage treatment) and tables of sources, effects and control. Study one unit at a time: read the notes, then close them and write each list from memory (the six natural resources, the parts of an ecosystem, the air pollutants and their effects). Finally answer the question bank on paper. Each unit has very short (2-mark), short answer (5-mark) and long essay (10-mark) questions, rated by how often that kind of question appears in PCI-syllabus papers.

**Units.** The syllabus has only three units of 10 hours each, and this pack follows them exactly, one notes file per unit; no unit was split or joined. Each unit is short in the syllabus but covers several topics, so the notes are a little longer than usual and are broken into numbered sections you can learn one at a time (for example Unit 1 has a separate section for each of the six natural resources, and Unit 3 a separate section for air, water and soil pollution).

## Exam pattern

BP206T is marked with an asterisk in the PCI B.Pharm regulations: it is a **non-university examination**, and the subject experts at college level conduct it. In the regulations' scheme of examination for semester II it carries:

| Part | Marks | Duration |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Continuous mode (attendance, academic activities, student–teacher interaction) | 10 | — |
| Sessional exams (set for 30 marks, converted to 15) | 15 | 1 hour each |
| **End-semester exam** | **50** | **2 hours** |
| Total | 75 | |

Sessional papers for non-university subjects are set for 30 marks (long answers 1 of 2 × 10, short answers 4 of 6 × 5); the average of two sessionals is converted to 15 marks.

**End-semester paper (50 marks, 2 hours).** The PCI regulations print this pattern for a 50-mark theory paper, and the full mock paper in this app follows it. There is **no MCQ section**, but the MCQs here are still good revision for definitions, dates of laws and examples. BP206T is a college-conducted exam, so **confirm the pattern with your college**.

| Section | What it asks | Marks |
| --- | --- | --- |
| I | Long answers — answer 2 of 3 | 2 × 10 = 20 |
| II | Short answers — answer 6 of 8 | 6 × 5 = 30 |
| | **Total** | **50** |

With three units and three long questions, expect roughly one long question from each unit and the eight short questions spread across all three. Time plan for two hours: about 25 minutes for each long answer and about 10 minutes for each short answer, leaving 10 minutes to read the paper and check.

There is no practical subject linked to BP206T.

## Probability ratings

- **High** — asked in most years; prepare the full answer with a diagram or table and examples.
- **Medium** — asked every few years or as part of a bigger question.
- **Low** — rare, but useful as a backup choice and for MCQ-style class tests.

These ratings are estimates from common patterns and syllabus weight, not a promise of what will be asked.

## Where the marks usually come from

| Unit | Topics that keep coming back |
| --- | --- |
| 1 Multidisciplinary nature and natural resources | Definition, scope and importance of environmental studies; renewable vs non-renewable resources; forest resources and deforestation; water resources, floods, drought and dams; mineral resources and effects of mining; food problems, fertiliser and pesticide problems; renewable energy sources; land degradation, soil erosion, desertification; role of an individual |
| 2 Ecosystems | Concept, structure and function; food chain, food web, energy flow (10% law); ecological pyramids; nitrogen and carbon cycles; ecological succession; forest, grassland, desert and aquatic ecosystems (pond, lake, river, ocean, estuary) |
| 3 Environmental pollution | Definition and classification of pollutants; air pollutants with sources and effects; acid rain, smog, greenhouse effect, ozone depletion; control devices (ESP, cyclone, scrubber, catalytic converter); water pollutants, eutrophication, BOD/COD/DO; sewage treatment; soil pollution, solid and biomedical waste management |

## Scoring tips for this subject

1. Begin every answer with a one-line definition, then write the points under small headings.
2. Draw something in every long answer: a food chain with arrows, an energy pyramid, the nitrogen or carbon cycle, the eutrophication sequence, a sewage treatment flow chart, or a labelled ESP or cyclone sketch.
3. Use the **source → effects → control** structure for any pollution question, and the **uses → problems → conservation** structure for any natural resource question.
4. Use tables for comparisons: renewable vs non-renewable, classical vs photochemical smog, BOD vs COD, grazing vs detritus food chain, primary vs secondary succession.
5. Quote Indian examples and laws: Chipko movement, Narmada dams, Bhopal gas tragedy, Thar desert, Sundarbans estuary, Water Act 1974, Air Act 1981, Environment (Protection) Act 1986.
6. Add a pharmacy link where it fits: medicinal plants from forests, pharmaceutical effluent, solvent vapours, antibiotic residues and resistance, biomedical waste and safe disposal of medicines.
7. A 10-mark answer needs about six to eight headed points plus a diagram or table and a short conclusion. A 5-mark answer needs about five clear points or a small table.
8. Finish pollution and resource answers with a line on what an individual can do; examiners reward it.

# Last-night revision sheet

If you only have an hour, learn these five answers in full, each with its diagram: **deforestation (causes, effects, conservation)**, **structure and function of an ecosystem with energy flow and pyramids**, **nitrogen cycle**, **air pollution (sources, effects, control devices)** and **water pollution with eutrophication and sewage treatment**. Together they cover most 10-mark questions.

## Unit 2 — Ecosystems

```text
Structure: abiotic (inorganic, organic, climatic) + biotic (producers, consumers, decomposers)
Function:  energy flow · nutrient cycling · productivity · succession

Sun → producers → herbivores → carnivores → top carnivores   (about 10% passes on each step)
```

| Point | Key fact |
| --- | --- |
| Ecosystem term | Tansley, 1935 |
| GPP / NPP | Total photosynthesis / GPP minus plant respiration |
| Energy flow | One-way; nutrients cycle |
| Food chains | Grazing (starts with green plants), detritus (starts with dead matter) |
| Food web | Interlinked chains; gives stability |
| Pyramid of energy | Always upright |
| Pyramid of numbers | Upright in grassland; spindle in tree chain; inverted in parasite chain |
| Pyramid of biomass | Inverted in pond and ocean |
| Nitrogen cycle | Fixation (*Rhizobium*, *Azotobacter*, lightning) → assimilation → ammonification → nitrification (*Nitrosomonas*, *Nitrobacter*) → denitrification |
| Biomagnification | Non-degradable, fat-soluble pollutants rise up the chain (DDT, mercury) |
| Succession | Pioneer → seral stages → climax; primary (bare rock) vs secondary (abandoned field) |
| Forest types | Tropical evergreen, deciduous, thorn, temperate coniferous, mangrove |
| Desert | Rainfall below about 25 cm a year; xerophytes; Thar (hot), Ladakh (cold) |
| Lake zones | Littoral, limnetic, profundal, benthic |
| Estuary | River meets sea; brackish; very productive; Sundarbans |

## Unit 3 — Pollution

| Pollutant | Source | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| CO | Vehicle exhaust | Carboxyhaemoglobin, less oxygen to tissues |
| SO2, NOx | Coal, vehicles | Respiratory irritation, acid rain |
| PM2.5 | Dust, smoke, stubble burning | Deep lung damage, heart disease |
| Ozone, PAN | Photochemical smog | Eye and lung irritation, crop damage |
| Lead | Smelters, batteries, old leaded petrol | Nerve damage in children |
| CFCs | Old refrigerants, aerosols | Ozone depletion |
| CO2, CH4, N2O | Fuels, farming | Global warming |

| Topic | Remember |
| --- | --- |
| Smog | Classical: smoke + SO2, cold fog; photochemical: NOx + hydrocarbons + sunlight |
| Acid rain | SO2 → H2SO4, NOx → HNO3; normal rain about pH 5.6 |
| Ozone depletion | Cl· chain reaction; Antarctic hole; Montreal Protocol 1987 |
| Particle control | Settling chamber, cyclone, bag filter, ESP, wet scrubber |
| Gas control | Absorption, adsorption (activated carbon), incineration, catalytic converter |
| DO / BOD / COD | DO high = clean; BOD 5 days at 20 °C; COD by dichromate; COD ≥ BOD |
| Eutrophication | Nutrients → algal bloom → oxygen loss → fish death |
| Heavy metal diseases | Minamata = mercury; itai-itai = cadmium; blue baby = nitrate; fluorosis = fluoride |
| Sewage treatment | Preliminary → primary → secondary (activated sludge, trickling filter) → tertiary → disinfection |
| Soil pollution control | 3 Rs, segregation, composting, sanitary landfill, incineration, bioremediation |
| Biomedical waste | Segregate at source into colour-coded containers; Bio-Medical Waste Management Rules 2016 |
| Laws | Water Act 1974, Air Act 1981, Environment (Protection) Act 1986 |
| Disaster example | Bhopal 1984, methyl isocyanate |

1. Food chain and energy pyramid with the 10% figures.
2. Nitrogen cycle with the bacteria named.
3. Eutrophication flow sequence.
4. Sewage treatment flow chart.

questions.answer:
1. Definition: scientific study of the environmental system and of natural and human-caused changes affecting organisms; includes physical, biological, social and cultural factors and human impact.
2. Components: lithosphere, hydrosphere, atmosphere, biosphere.
3. Multidisciplinary nature: biology (organisms, food chains), chemistry (pollutants, reactions), physics (energy, radiation), geology and geography (soil, minerals, climate), engineering (treatment plants, control devices), economics (costs, valuing resources), law (environmental acts), sociology and ethics (people's attitudes), medicine and pharmacy (health effects, drug residues). Example: a river polluted by a factory needs all of these.
4. Scope: conservation of resources, ecosystems and biodiversity, pollution control and waste management, environmental impact assessment, law and policy, careers in pollution control boards and industry.
5. Importance: resources are limited and demand grows; global problems (warming, ozone depletion); health effects of pollution; sustainable development.
6. Need for public awareness: laws succeed only with public support; individual habits (saving water and energy, segregating waste, safe disposal of medicines) add up; people's movements such as Chipko protect resources.
7. Conclusion: environmental protection is everyone's responsibility.
questions.question: Define environmental studies. Explain its multidisciplinary nature, scope and importance, and the need for public awareness.

questions.answer:
1. Forests: land areas dominated by trees; India aims for one-third of land under forest (National Forest Policy 1988).
2. Productive uses: timber, fuelwood, paper pulp, bamboo, food, fodder, medicinal plants (rauwolfia, cinchona, neem), gums, resins, tannins, essential oils.
3. Protective uses: oxygen production and CO2 absorption, soil conservation, regulation of rainfall and groundwater recharge, habitat for wildlife, flood control, climate moderation.
4. Causes of deforestation: agriculture and shifting cultivation, fuelwood and timber, urban and industrial growth, roads, mining, dams, overgrazing, fires.
5. Effects: soil erosion and landslides, silting, floods and droughts, loss of biodiversity and medicinal plants, global warming, change in rainfall, desertification, loss of tribal livelihood.
6. Timber extraction: logging removes best trees, opens canopy, roads bring further clearing.
7. Mining: removes vegetation and topsoil, leaves pits and dumps, pollutes streams.
8. Dams: submerge forests and villages; displace tribal people with poor rehabilitation (Narmada protests).
9. Conservation: afforestation, social forestry, Joint Forest Management, protected areas, alternative fuels, Chipko movement.
questions.question: What are forest resources? Describe their uses, the causes and effects of deforestation, and the effects of timber extraction, mining and dams on forests and tribal people.

questions.answer:
1. About 97% of earth's water is saline; usable fresh water is a small fraction, most fresh water being frozen.
2. Uses: domestic, irrigation (largest use in India), industry including pharmaceutical purified water, power, fisheries.
3. Over-utilisation: falling water table, wells drying, land subsidence, salt-water intrusion in coastal aquifers, drying rivers, water logging and salinity, less water to dilute pollution.
4. Floods: heavy rain, cloud bursts, snow melt; worsened by deforestation and loss of wetlands; loss of life, crops and homes, water-borne diseases.
5. Drought: prolonged deficit of rainfall; monsoon failure, deforestation, overuse of groundwater; crop failure, water and fodder shortage, migration.
6. Conflicts: inter-state river disputes (Cauvery, Krishna); international sharing of rivers by treaty; competition between farms, industry and cities.
7. Dams — benefits: irrigation, hydroelectricity, drinking water, flood control, fisheries.
8. Dams — problems: submergence of forests and villages, displacement of people, silting, water logging and salinity, water-borne disease, reduced downstream flow, dam-failure risk.
9. Conservation: rainwater harvesting, watershed management, drip irrigation, reuse of treated water.
questions.question: Discuss water resources with reference to over-utilisation of surface and groundwater, floods, drought, conflicts over water, and the benefits and problems of dams.

questions.answer: Renewable resources are replaced by natural processes within a human time scale if used wisely: forests, water, fish, crops, solar and wind energy. Non-renewable resources take millions of years to form and cannot be replaced once used: coal, petroleum, natural gas, metal ores, uranium. Renewable resources become exhausted if used faster than they regenerate (over-pumped groundwater, over-cut forest). Non-renewable resources must be conserved by efficient use, recycling and substitution with renewables. Inexhaustible resources such as sunlight and wind never run out.
questions.question: Differentiate renewable and non-renewable resources with examples.

questions.answer:
1. Destruction of vegetation and topsoil; scarred land, pits and waste dumps.
2. Dust and gases from mining and crushing; lung diseases such as silicosis and coal dust disease in miners.
3. Acid mine drainage: water through sulphide ores becomes acidic and carries heavy metals into streams.
4. Lowering and contamination of groundwater.
5. Land subsidence over underground mines; landslides on waste heaps.
6. Smelting releases SO2, particulates and toxic metals.
7. Displacement of people, loss of farmland and forest.
Remedies: reclamation and re-planting of mined land, treatment of mine water, recycling of metals, eco-friendly mining methods.
questions.question: Describe the environmental effects of extracting and using mineral resources.

questions.answer:
1. Fertilisers: excess nitrate leaches into groundwater (blue baby syndrome in infants); runoff of nitrate and phosphate causes eutrophication of lakes; soil micro-organisms decline.
2. Pesticides: kill useful insects and pollinators; pests develop resistance; persistent pesticides such as DDT biomagnify in food chains; residues in food.
3. Water logging: over-irrigation without drainage raises the water table so roots lack air and crops fail.
4. Salinity: irrigation water evaporates leaving salts at the surface, making land barren.
5. Loss of genetic diversity as a few high-yielding varieties replace traditional ones.
Remedies: integrated pest management, biofertilisers, organic manure, balanced fertiliser use, drip irrigation, proper drainage.
questions.question: Explain the effects of modern agriculture: fertiliser and pesticide problems, water logging and salinity.

questions.answer: Energy demand grows with population and industry, and fossil fuels are limited and polluting. Alternative sources: (1) Solar — solar cells and heaters; (2) Wind — wind turbines; (3) Hydropower — falling water; (4) Biomass and biogas — gas from cow dung and organic waste, useful in villages; (5) Geothermal — heat from inside the earth; (6) Tidal and wave energy; (7) Hydrogen in fuel cells. Advantages: do not run out, little pollution, local use. Limitations: high initial cost, dependence on weather, need for storage. Energy conservation (efficient appliances, public transport) is equally important.
questions.question: Write a note on renewable (alternative) sources of energy.

questions.answer: Land degradation is the decline in quality and productivity of land. Soil erosion is removal of fertile topsoil by water (sheet, rill, gully erosion) or wind; causes are deforestation, overgrazing and poor farming; control by afforestation, contour ploughing, terracing, strip cropping and windbreaks. Man-induced landslides result from road and dam building on steep slopes, blasting, mining and removal of trees, especially in the Himalaya and Western Ghats. Desertification is the conversion of fertile dry land into desert-like land through overgrazing, deforestation and poor irrigation, as in the Thar region; controlled by afforestation, controlled grazing and water conservation.
questions.question: What is land degradation? Explain soil erosion, man-induced landslides and desertification.

questions.answer: Development that meets the needs of the present generation without reducing the ability of future generations to meet their own needs.
questions.question: What is sustainable development?

questions.answer: A people's movement of the 1970s in the Garhwal Himalaya in which villagers, many of them women, hugged trees to stop them from being felled; it became a symbol of forest conservation in India.
questions.question: What was the Chipko movement?

questions.answer: Any two: saving water (closing taps, fixing leaks, rainwater harvesting); saving energy (switching off lights, using LED bulbs, public transport); practising reduce, reuse, recycle; planting trees; returning unused medicines to a take-back point instead of throwing them in drains.
questions.question: Write two roles of an individual in conserving natural resources.

questions.answer:
1. Definition: a community of organisms interacting with each other and with their non-living surroundings as a self-supporting unit through which energy flows and nutrients cycle (term by Tansley, 1935).
2. Abiotic components: inorganic substances (water, CO2, O2, N, P, minerals); organic substances (carbohydrates, proteins, lipids, humus); climatic factors (light, temperature, rainfall, humidity, pH).
3. Biotic components: producers (green plants, algae — photosynthesis); consumers — primary (herbivores), secondary (carnivores), tertiary (top carnivores), omnivores; decomposers (bacteria and fungi) returning nutrients.
4. Diagram: ecosystem → abiotic and biotic branches.
5. Functions: energy flow through food chains and webs (one-way, about 10% passed on); nutrient cycling (carbon, nitrogen, water, phosphorus); productivity (GPP, NPP); regulation and succession towards a climax community.
6. Example: pond — phytoplankton → zooplankton → small fish → large fish, with bacteria in the mud.
7. Conclusion: balance between components keeps the ecosystem stable.
questions.question: Define an ecosystem. Describe the structure and functions of an ecosystem with suitable examples.

questions.answer:
1. Sun is the source of energy; producers fix a small part by photosynthesis.
2. Energy flow is unidirectional; at each trophic level most energy is lost as heat in respiration; about 10% passes to the next level (Lindeman's ten per cent law); so chains have only 4–5 links.
3. Food chain: sequence of eating and being eaten; grazing chain (grass → grasshopper → frog → snake → eagle) and detritus chain (leaf litter → earthworm → bird).
4. Food web: interlinked chains; provides stability since predators have alternative prey.
5. Pyramid of numbers: upright in grassland; spindle-shaped in a tree food chain; inverted in a parasite chain.
6. Pyramid of biomass: upright on land; inverted in pond and ocean (small mass of fast-growing phytoplankton).
7. Pyramid of energy: always upright.
8. Diagrams: energy flow chain with 10% figures and a pyramid.
9. Biomagnification of DDT and mercury up the chain as an application.
questions.question: Explain energy flow in an ecosystem. Describe food chains, food webs and ecological pyramids with diagrams.

questions.answer:
1. Aquatic ecosystems: freshwater (pond, lake, stream, river) and marine (ocean); estuary where they meet.
2. Pond: small, shallow, still water; producers — phytoplankton, Hydrilla, floating plants; consumers — zooplankton, snails, small fish, frogs, large fish, kingfisher; decomposers in mud.
3. Lake: larger, deeper; zones — littoral (shallow, rooted plants), limnetic (open lit water), profundal (deep, dark), benthic (bottom); oligotrophic vs eutrophic lakes.
4. Stream and river: flowing water, high oxygen, organisms adapted to current; rivers carry silt and nutrients, form fertile plains.
5. Ocean: covers about 71% of earth; zones — intertidal, photic (phytoplankton), aphotic deep sea; coral reefs; provides food, oxygen, climate regulation, minerals, marine drug sources.
6. Estuary: river mouth, brackish water with changing salinity; very productive; mangroves, fish nurseries; Sundarbans.
7. Threats: pollution, eutrophication, over-fishing, reclamation.
questions.question: Describe the introduction, types, characteristic features, structure and function of aquatic ecosystems (pond, lake, river, ocean and estuary).

questions.answer: Air is about 78% N2, but most organisms cannot use it directly. (1) Nitrogen fixation: N2 converted to ammonia/nitrogen compounds by Rhizobium in legume nodules, Azotobacter, blue-green algae, lightning and industrial fertiliser manufacture. (2) Assimilation: plants absorb nitrate and ammonium and build proteins; animals eat plants. (3) Ammonification: decomposers convert dead matter and wastes to ammonia. (4) Nitrification: Nitrosomonas oxidises ammonia to nitrite and Nitrobacter nitrite to nitrate. (5) Denitrification: bacteria such as Pseudomonas reduce nitrate to N2, returning it to air. Diagram: air N2 → fixation → soil nitrate → plants → animals → dead matter → ammonia → nitrite → nitrate → back to N2.
questions.question: Describe the nitrogen cycle with a diagram.

questions.answer: Ecological pyramids show the relationship between trophic levels with producers at the base. Pyramid of numbers: number of organisms per level; upright in grassland, spindle in a tree food chain, inverted in a parasite chain. Pyramid of biomass: dry mass per level; upright on land, inverted in pond and ocean because a small standing crop of rapidly multiplying phytoplankton supports a larger mass of consumers. Pyramid of energy: energy flow per unit time; always upright because energy is lost as heat at every level and only about 10% passes to the next, so a higher level can never have more energy than the one below.
questions.question: Explain ecological pyramids. Why is the pyramid of energy always upright?

questions.answer: Forests are land ecosystems dominated by trees. Types: tropical evergreen (Western Ghats, north-east), tropical deciduous (teak, sal), thorn forest, temperate coniferous (Himalayan pine, deodar), mangrove (Sundarbans). Structure: producers — trees, shrubs, herbs; primary consumers — insects, deer, squirrels, elephants; secondary and tertiary consumers — snakes, foxes, tigers, hawks; decomposers — fungi and bacteria in leaf litter. Functions: high productivity, carbon storage, regulation of climate and water, soil protection, timber, food and medicinal plants, home for tribal people.
questions.question: Write a note on the forest ecosystem.

questions.answer: Grassland: dominated by grasses, rainfall too low for forest; types — savanna, prairie, steppe, pampas, alpine meadow; producers grasses and herbs; consumers cattle, deer, rabbits, grasshoppers, frogs, snakes, hawks; threatened by overgrazing and farming. Desert: very low rainfall (usually under about 25 cm a year), high evaporation, hot days and cold nights in hot deserts; types hot (Thar) and cold (Ladakh); producers xerophytes such as cacti and acacia with thick cuticles, spines, fleshy stems and deep roots; consumers insects, reptiles, rodents, camels and foxes active mainly at night; few decomposers.
questions.question: Describe the grassland and desert ecosystems.

questions.answer: Ecological succession is the gradual, orderly replacement of one community by another in an area until a stable climax community develops. Primary succession begins on bare ground with no previous life (bare rock, new pond); secondary succession begins where vegetation was removed but soil remains (abandoned field, burnt forest) and is faster. Hydrosere starts in water, xerosere on dry rock. Stages: pioneer species (lichens on rock, phytoplankton in water) → seral stages (mosses, grasses, shrubs) → climax community (forest). The whole sequence is a sere.
questions.question: What is ecological succession? Explain its types and stages.

questions.answer: A food chain is a sequence of organisms in which each eats the one before it (grass → grasshopper → frog). A food web is a network of interconnected food chains in an ecosystem.
questions.question: Define food chain and food web.

questions.answer: Proposed by Lindeman: on average only about 10% of the energy at one trophic level is transferred to the next; the rest is lost mainly as heat.
questions.question: What is the ten per cent law?

questions.answer: A partly enclosed coastal area where a river meets the sea, so fresh and salt water mix to form brackish water; it is highly productive (example: Sundarbans).
questions.question: What is an estuary?

questions.answer:
1. Definition: presence in air of contaminants in amounts and for durations that harm humans, animals, plants or property.
2. Sources: natural (volcanoes, dust storms, forest fires, pollen); man-made — vehicles, thermal power plants, industries including pharmaceutical (solvent vapours), domestic burning, stubble burning, waste burning.
3. Pollutants and effects: CO → carboxyhaemoglobin, hypoxia; SO2 and NOx → respiratory irritation, acid rain, plant damage; particulate matter PM10/PM2.5 → asthma, bronchitis, heart disease; hydrocarbons/VOCs (benzene carcinogenic); ozone and PAN → eye and lung irritation; lead → nerve damage; CFCs → ozone depletion; CO2 → global warming.
4. Effects on materials: corrosion, damage to marble monuments, soot.
5. Control at source: cleaner fuels (CNG, LPG, low-sulphur diesel), emission norms, maintenance, process change and solvent recovery, green belts.
6. Particle control: gravity settling chamber, cyclone separator, bag filter, electrostatic precipitator, wet scrubber.
7. Gas control: absorption, adsorption on activated carbon, incineration, catalytic converter.
8. Law: Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act 1981, Environment (Protection) Act 1986; Bhopal 1984 as a lesson.
questions.question: Define air pollution. Discuss the sources, major pollutants and their effects, and methods of controlling air pollution.

questions.answer:
1. Definition: change in physical, chemical or biological quality of water making it harmful or unfit for use.
2. Sources: domestic sewage, industrial effluent (pharmaceutical, tannery, textile, chemical), agricultural runoff, hospitals, power plants (thermal pollution), oil spills, mining, landfill leachate; point and non-point sources.
3. Pollutants and effects: pathogens → cholera, typhoid, hepatitis A; organic wastes → oxygen depletion, fish death; nutrients → eutrophication, blue baby syndrome; heavy metals → Minamata (mercury), itai-itai (cadmium), arsenicosis; pesticides → biomagnification; drug residues → antibiotic resistance; oil; heat; fluoride → fluorosis.
4. Eutrophication sequence: nutrients → algal bloom → decay → low DO → fish death.
5. Measurement: DO, BOD (5 days, 20 °C), COD (dichromate), coliforms.
6. Treatment: preliminary (screens, grit) → primary sedimentation → secondary biological (activated sludge, trickling filter, oxidation pond) → tertiary (nutrient removal, carbon, RO) → disinfection; sludge digestion.
7. Other control: less fertiliser, no dumping of waste or medicines, reuse of water, Water Act 1974.
questions.question: Define water pollution. Describe its sources, types of pollutants and their effects, and the methods of control including wastewater treatment.

questions.answer:
1. Definition: chemicals or other substances in soil at levels that reduce fertility, harm soil life or enter food and groundwater.
2. Sources: excess fertilisers and pesticides, industrial waste and sludge, urban solid waste and plastics, biomedical waste, e-waste, mining tailings, irrigation with sewage, acid rain, radioactive waste.
3. Effects: loss of fertility and soil organisms, toxic residues in crops, groundwater contamination, change in pH and salinity, disease from open dumps, plastics blocking drains and harming animals.
4. Control: 3 Rs; segregation at source; composting and vermicomposting; sanitary landfill with liner and daily cover; incineration of hazardous waste; bioremediation and phytoremediation; balanced fertiliser use and integrated pest management; afforestation.
5. Biomedical waste: segregate at point of generation into colour-coded containers (yellow, red, white puncture-proof, blue) under the Bio-Medical Waste Management Rules 2016; treat at an authorised common facility; expired medicines must not go to garbage or drains; pharmacist runs take-back and educates patients.
6. Laws: Environment (Protection) Act 1986 and waste management rules.
questions.question: Explain soil pollution: its sources, effects and control. Add a note on solid and biomedical waste management.

questions.answer: Sunlight warms the earth, which radiates heat as infrared. Greenhouse gases (CO2, methane, nitrous oxide, CFCs, water vapour) absorb part of this heat and keep the earth warm — the natural greenhouse effect. Extra greenhouse gases from burning fossil fuels, deforestation and farming trap more heat, causing global warming. Effects: rising temperature, melting glaciers and polar ice, sea-level rise, extreme weather, crop changes, spread of vector-borne diseases. Control: renewable energy, energy efficiency, afforestation, international agreements (Kyoto Protocol 1997, Paris Agreement 2015).
questions.question: Write a note on the greenhouse effect and global warming.

questions.answer: The stratospheric ozone layer absorbs harmful UV-B radiation. CFCs and other halogen compounds release chlorine atoms under UV light; Cl· reacts with O3 to form ClO· and O2, and ClO· reacts with atomic oxygen to free Cl· again, so one chlorine atom destroys many ozone molecules. A seasonal ozone hole appears over Antarctica. Effects of more UV-B: skin cancer, cataract, weakened immunity, damage to crops and plankton. Control: Montreal Protocol (1987) phased out CFCs; CFC propellants in metered-dose inhalers were replaced by HFAs; safe disposal of old refrigerants.
questions.question: What is ozone layer depletion? Give its causes, effects and control.

questions.answer: Acid rain is rain with a pH below that of normal rain (about 5.6). SO2 from coal burning and smelting and NOx from vehicles and power plants react with oxygen and water in the air to form sulphuric and nitric acids, which fall as rain, snow or fog. Effects: acidification of lakes and death of fish; leaching of soil nutrients and damage to forests; release of toxic aluminium from soil; corrosion of metals and erosion of marble and limestone buildings and monuments. Control: low-sulphur fuels, scrubbers, catalytic converters, emission limits.
questions.question: What is acid rain? Explain its formation and effects.

questions.answer: DO (dissolved oxygen) is the oxygen dissolved in water; high DO indicates healthy water, low DO heavy organic pollution. BOD (biochemical oxygen demand) is the oxygen used by micro-organisms to break down organic matter in a sample, usually measured over 5 days at 20 °C; high BOD means much biodegradable organic pollution. COD (chemical oxygen demand) is the oxygen needed to oxidise all organic matter chemically using potassium dichromate in acid; it includes matter microbes cannot degrade, so COD is equal to or more than BOD. These values are used to judge water quality and the efficiency of effluent treatment.
questions.question: Define BOD, COD and DO. What is their significance in water pollution?

questions.answer: Electrostatic precipitator: polluted gas passes between discharge electrodes at high voltage and earthed collecting plates; particles become charged and are attracted to the collecting plates; plates are rapped so dust falls into hoppers; removes very fine particles with high efficiency; used in thermal power plants and cement works. Cyclone separator: gas enters a cylindrical-conical chamber tangentially and spins; centrifugal force throws heavier particles against the wall, they slide down and are collected at the bottom while clean gas leaves through a central outlet; simple and cheap but less efficient for very fine particles.
questions.question: Describe the electrostatic precipitator and cyclone separator used in air pollution control.

questions.answer: Classical smog forms in cold, humid, foggy weather from smoke and SO2 of coal burning; it is reducing in nature and forms sulphuric acid droplets and soot; it causes bronchitis and deaths in the elderly. Photochemical smog forms in warm, sunny, dry weather when NOx and hydrocarbons from vehicles react in sunlight; it is oxidising and produces ozone, PAN and aldehydes; it causes eye irritation, respiratory problems and plant damage. Control of both: cleaner fuels, emission control and catalytic converters.
questions.question: Compare classical (London) smog and photochemical smog.

questions.answer: Excessive enrichment of a water body with nutrients (nitrates and phosphates) causing algal blooms, which on decaying use up dissolved oxygen and kill fish and other aquatic life.
questions.question: What is eutrophication?

questions.answer: The increase in concentration of a non-degradable, fat-soluble pollutant (such as DDT or mercury) at each successive level of a food chain, so top predators carry the highest levels.
questions.question: What is biomagnification?

questions.answer: Mercury (methyl mercury in fish) causes Minamata disease; cadmium causes itai-itai disease.
questions.question: Name the diseases caused by mercury and cadmium pollution of water.

# Unit 1: Multidisciplinary nature of environmental studies and natural resources

Everything a pharmacist uses comes from the environment: water for manufacturing, plants for crude drugs, minerals for inorganic compounds, energy to run the plant. This unit explains what environmental studies covers, why it draws on many subjects, and how each natural resource is used, overused and protected.

## 1.1 The environment and environmental studies

**Environment** is the sum of all living and non-living surroundings that affect an organism: air, water, soil, other plants and animals, and the social and cultural setting created by people. The word comes from the French *environner*, "to surround".

The environment has four connected parts (spheres):

| Sphere | What it is | Examples |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Lithosphere | Solid crust of the earth: rocks, soil, minerals | Mountains, farmland, ores |
| Hydrosphere | All water on, under and above the earth | Oceans, rivers, groundwater, glaciers, clouds |
| Atmosphere | Layer of gases held around the earth by gravity | Nitrogen, oxygen, carbon dioxide, water vapour |
| Biosphere | The thin zone where life exists, overlapping the other three | Forests, oceans, soil organisms, people |

```text
            Atmosphere
           /          \
  Lithosphere ---- Hydrosphere
           \          /
            Biosphere  (life exists where the three meet)
```

**Environmental studies** (environmental science) is the scientific study of the environmental system and of the changes, natural or caused by people, that affect organisms. It covers the physical and biological features of the environment and also the social and cultural factors and the impact of humans on it.

## 1.2 Multidisciplinary nature

No single subject can explain an environmental problem. Take a river polluted by a drug factory: chemistry identifies the effluent, biology shows the harm to fish, engineering designs the treatment plant, economics weighs the cost, law sets the discharge limits, and sociology explains why villagers downstream are affected. That is why environmental studies is called **multidisciplinary** (or interdisciplinary).

| Discipline | What it contributes |
| --- | --- |
| Biology, botany, zoology, microbiology | Living organisms, food chains, biodiversity, biodegradation |
| Chemistry and biochemistry | Composition of air, water and soil; reactions of pollutants; toxicity |
| Physics | Energy flow, radiation, heat balance, movement of pollutants |
| Geology and geography | Rocks, soil formation, minerals, landforms, climate zones, mapping |
| Mathematics and statistics | Models, sampling, data analysis, forecasting |
| Engineering and technology | Pollution control devices, waste treatment, renewable energy |
| Economics | Cost of damage and control, valuing resources, sustainable development |
| Law and political science | Environmental acts, rules, international treaties |
| Sociology, ethics, education | Public attitudes, people's movements, awareness |
| Medicine and pharmacy | Health effects of pollution, safe disposal of medicines, drug residues in water |

### Scope of environmental studies

- Conservation and wise use of natural resources.
- Understanding ecosystems and biodiversity.
- Control of pollution and management of wastes.
- Environmental impact assessment of new projects (dams, factories, roads).
- Environmental law, policy and management.
- Research and jobs: pollution control boards, effluent treatment, environmental consultancy, green chemistry in industry.

### Importance and need for public awareness

1. Resources are limited while population and demand keep growing.
2. Many problems (global warming, ozone depletion, plastic waste) are global and need everyone's action.
3. Pollution harms health directly: respiratory disease, water-borne infection, poisoning by heavy metals.
4. Laws work only when citizens understand and support them.
5. Development must be **sustainable**: meet today's needs without reducing the ability of future generations to meet theirs.
6. Awareness changes daily habits: saving water and power, segregating waste, returning unused medicines rather than flushing them.

## 1.3 Natural resources

A **natural resource** is anything obtained from nature that people use to meet their needs: air, water, soil, minerals, forests, wildlife, fossil fuels and sunlight.

### Classification

| Type | Meaning | Examples |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Renewable** | Replaced by natural processes within a human time scale, if not overused | Forests, water, fish, crops, soil (slowly), solar and wind energy |
| **Non-renewable** | Formed over millions of years; once used up they are gone for practical purposes | Coal, petroleum, natural gas, metal ores |
| Inexhaustible | Will not run out whatever we use | Sunlight, wind, tides |
| Exhaustible | Can be used up | Fossil fuels, minerals; also renewables when overused |

A renewable resource becomes effectively non-renewable when it is used faster than it is replaced: cutting a forest faster than it regrows, or pumping groundwater faster than rain refills it.

```text
Natural resources
├── Renewable ........ forests, water, food, soil, wildlife, solar/wind energy
└── Non-renewable .... fossil fuels (coal, oil, gas), minerals, nuclear fuels
```

## 1.4 Forest resources

About a third of India's land should be under forest according to the National Forest Policy of 1988, but actual cover is well below this.

### Uses of forests

| Productive (direct) uses | Protective (indirect) uses |
| --- | --- |
| Timber and fuelwood | Produce oxygen and absorb carbon dioxide |
| Paper pulp, bamboo, cane | Hold soil and prevent erosion and landslides |
| Food: fruits, honey, nuts | Regulate rainfall and the water cycle; recharge groundwater |
| **Medicinal plants** and crude drugs (for example rauwolfia, cinchona, neem) | Home to wildlife; protect biodiversity |
| Gums, resins, tannins, dyes, essential oils | Moderate local climate; reduce floods |
| Fodder for cattle; livelihood of tribal people | Recreation, tourism, research |

### Over-exploitation and deforestation

**Deforestation** is the permanent removal of forest for other uses.

**Causes**

- Clearing for agriculture, including shifting (jhum) cultivation in the north-east.
- Fuelwood collection and commercial timber logging.
- Expansion of cities, roads, railways and industries.
- Mining and quarrying.
- Large dams that submerge forest land.
- Overgrazing, forest fires, and pests and diseases.

**Effects**

- Soil erosion, landslides and silting of rivers and reservoirs.
- More floods and droughts; falling groundwater.
- Loss of habitat and extinction of plants and animals, including medicinal species.
- Less carbon absorbed, which adds to global warming.
- Change in local rainfall and climate; spread of deserts.
- Loss of livelihood for forest dwellers.

### Timber extraction, mining and dams

- **Timber extraction:** large-scale logging removes the best trees, damages young ones, opens the canopy and builds roads that bring further clearing.
- **Mining:** open-cast mining removes all vegetation and topsoil, leaves pits and waste dumps, and pollutes nearby streams.
- **Dams:** reservoirs submerge forests and villages. Tribal and rural people lose their land and are displaced, often with poor rehabilitation. The protests over the Narmada (Sardar Sarovar) project are a well-known Indian example.

### Conservation of forests

- Afforestation and reforestation; social forestry and agroforestry.
- Joint Forest Management, where villagers protect forests and share benefits.
- Protected areas: national parks, sanctuaries, biosphere reserves.
- Use of alternative fuels (biogas, LPG) to reduce fuelwood demand.
- Controlled grazing and fire control.
- People's movements: the **Chipko movement** of the 1970s in the Garhwal Himalaya, where villagers, many of them women, hugged trees to stop felling.

## 1.5 Water resources

Water covers most of the earth's surface, but about 97% of it is salt water in the oceans. Only about 3% is fresh, and most of that is locked in ice caps and glaciers, so the water readily available in lakes, rivers and shallow groundwater is a very small fraction.

### Uses

Drinking and domestic use, irrigation (the largest use in India), industry (cooling, processing, pharmaceutical manufacture as purified water and water for injection), hydroelectric power, transport, fisheries and recreation.

### Over-utilisation of surface and groundwater

| Problem | Explanation |
| --- | --- |
| Falling water table | Pumping from tube wells faster than recharge; wells run dry |
| Ground subsidence | Land sinks when water is removed from below |
| Salt-water intrusion | In coastal areas, sea water moves into emptied aquifers |
| Drying of rivers and lakes | Excess withdrawal for irrigation and cities |
| Water logging and salinity | Over-irrigation raises the water table and salts collect at the surface |
| Pollution | Less water to dilute the waste that enters it |

### Floods and drought

- **Floods:** heavy rain, melting snow, cloud bursts or dam bursts make water overflow its banks. Deforestation and loss of wetlands make floods worse because water runs off faster. Effects: loss of life and crops, damage to homes, water-borne diseases.
- **Drought:** a long period of rainfall well below normal. Causes include failure of the monsoon, deforestation and overuse of groundwater. Effects: crop failure, shortage of drinking water and fodder, migration, famine.

### Conflicts over water

When rivers cross state or national borders, sharing their water causes disputes. Examples in India are disputes between states over the Cauvery, Krishna and other rivers; internationally, sharing of the Indus and Ganga waters is governed by treaties. Within a region, farmers, industries and cities compete for the same water.

### Dams: benefits and problems

| Benefits | Problems |
| --- | --- |
| Irrigation water for dry areas | Submergence of forests, farmland and villages |
| Hydroelectric power | Displacement of people, mostly poor and tribal |
| Drinking water supply | Silting of the reservoir, shortening its life |
| Flood control | Water logging and salinity in command areas |
| Fisheries, navigation, recreation | Spread of water-borne diseases; loss of downstream flow |
| | Possible earthquakes and the risk of dam failure |

### Conservation of water

Rainwater harvesting, check dams and watershed management, drip and sprinkler irrigation, repair of leaks, reuse of treated wastewater, protecting wetlands, and treating effluent before discharge.

## 1.6 Mineral resources

**Minerals** are naturally occurring inorganic substances with a definite composition, found in rocks. **Ores** are minerals from which a metal can be extracted profitably.

### Uses

| Mineral | Use |
| --- | --- |
| Iron, aluminium, copper | Construction, machines, utensils, wires |
| Coal and petroleum | Fuel, power generation, petrochemicals |
| Limestone, gypsum | Cement, building |
| Uranium | Nuclear power |
| Gold, silver, diamonds | Jewellery, electronics |
| Sulphur, phosphate, potash | Fertilisers, chemicals |
| Talc, kaolin, bentonite, calcium carbonate | **Pharmaceutical excipients**, cosmetics |

### Environmental effects of extracting and using minerals

- **Mining** destroys vegetation and topsoil; creates pits, waste dumps and scarred land.
- Dust and gases pollute air; miners suffer lung diseases (for example silicosis, black lung from coal dust).
- Acid mine drainage: water passing through sulphide ores becomes acidic and carries heavy metals into rivers.
- Groundwater lowered or contaminated.
- Subsidence of land over underground mines; landslides on waste heaps.
- **Processing (smelting)** releases sulphur dioxide, particulate matter and toxic metals.
- Displacement of people and loss of farmland.

**Remedies:** environment-friendly mining methods, refilling and re-planting mined land (reclamation), treating mine water, recycling metals, using substitutes.

## 1.7 Food resources

Food comes from crops, livestock and fisheries. The main food crops in India are rice, wheat, maize, millets and pulses.

### World food problems

- Rising population needs more food each year.
- Malnutrition and under-nutrition in poor regions, while food is wasted elsewhere.
- Loss of farmland to cities and land degradation.
- Climate change, drought and floods reduce yields.
- Poor storage and distribution; poverty limits access to food.

### Changes caused by agriculture and overgrazing

- **Overgrazing:** too many animals on a pasture remove plant cover, compact soil, expose it to erosion and can lead to desertification.
- **Agriculture:** clearing of natural vegetation, loss of wild species, soil erosion and nutrient loss.

### Effects of modern agriculture

The **Green Revolution** (high-yielding varieties, fertilisers, pesticides and irrigation) raised food production but brought problems:

| Problem | Explanation |
| --- | --- |
| Fertiliser problems | Excess nitrate leaches into groundwater; runoff of nitrate and phosphate causes **eutrophication** of lakes; soil micro-life declines |
| Pesticide problems | Kill useful insects; pests develop resistance; residues persist and **biomagnify** in food chains (DDT is the classic example) |
| Water logging | Over-irrigation raises the water table so roots cannot get air |
| Salinity | Salts brought up by irrigation water collect at the surface as water evaporates |
| Loss of genetic diversity | A few high-yielding varieties replace many traditional ones |

**Remedies:** integrated pest management, biofertilisers and organic manure, crop rotation, balanced fertiliser use, drip irrigation, good drainage.

## 1.8 Energy resources

Energy demand grows with population, industry, transport and living standards. Most of the world's commercial energy still comes from fossil fuels.

| Non-renewable sources | Renewable (alternative) sources |
| --- | --- |
| Coal | Solar energy (solar cells, solar heaters) |
| Petroleum (crude oil) | Wind energy |
| Natural gas | Hydropower |
| Nuclear fuels (uranium) | Biomass and **biogas** (from cow dung and organic waste) |
| | Geothermal energy |
| | Tidal and wave energy |
| | Hydrogen (fuel cells) |

**Problems with fossil fuels:** limited reserves, air pollution (SO2, NOx, particulates), carbon dioxide emissions causing global warming, oil spills. **Nuclear energy** produces little CO2 but raises concerns about radioactive waste and accidents.

**Advantages of renewable sources:** do not run out, cause little pollution, can be used locally in villages. Their limits are high initial cost, dependence on weather and the need for storage.

**Energy conservation:** use efficient lights and appliances, switch off when not needed, use public transport, insulate buildings, and design processes (including in pharmaceutical plants) to recover heat.

## 1.9 Land resources

Land supports farming, forests, homes, industry and wildlife, but its area is fixed.

### Land degradation

**Land degradation** is the decline in the quality and productivity of land. Causes: soil erosion, salinity and water logging, over-use of chemicals, mining, dumping of waste, deforestation and overgrazing.

### Man-induced landslides

Building roads and dams on steep hills, blasting, mining and removing trees weaken slopes, so rock and soil slide down, especially in the rainy season. The Himalayan and Western Ghats regions are prone to them.

### Soil erosion

**Soil erosion** is the removal of fertile topsoil by water or wind. Forms of water erosion include sheet, rill and gully erosion.

- Causes: deforestation, overgrazing, poor farming (ploughing down the slope), heavy rain on bare soil.
- Control: planting trees and grass, contour ploughing, terracing on slopes, strip cropping, windbreaks (shelter belts), check dams, keeping a plant cover.

### Desertification

**Desertification** is the process by which fertile land in dry regions turns into desert-like land because of climate variation and human activity (overgrazing, deforestation, poor irrigation). The Thar region of Rajasthan is the main area at risk in India. Control: afforestation, controlled grazing, water conservation and sand-dune stabilisation.

## 1.10 Role of an individual in conserving natural resources

| Resource | What one person can do |
| --- | --- |
| Water | Turn off taps, fix leaks, reuse water for plants, harvest rainwater |
| Energy | Switch off lights and fans, use LED bulbs, use public transport or cycle |
| Forests and paper | Use both sides of paper, recycle, plant and care for trees |
| Food | Avoid waste, buy local and seasonal food, prefer organic manure in gardens |
| Land and soil | Avoid plastics, compost kitchen waste, segregate waste at home |
| Medicines | Return expired or unused medicines to a take-back point instead of throwing them in drains or open dumps |
| General | Spread awareness, support conservation laws, practise the 3 Rs: reduce, reuse, recycle |

**Equitable use of resources:** rich countries and people use a far larger share of resources than poor ones. Sustainable development needs the rich to cut waste and the poor to have fair access.

## Remember

- Environmental studies is multidisciplinary: science, engineering, economics, law and sociology all contribute.
- Renewable resources can be replaced; non-renewable ones cannot. Overuse makes a renewable resource behave like a non-renewable one.
- Deforestation → erosion, floods, loss of biodiversity and medicinal plants, global warming.
- About 97% of earth's water is saline; usable fresh water is a tiny fraction.
- Dams give water and power but displace people and submerge forests.
- Mining causes land damage, dust, acid mine drainage and lung disease.
- Modern agriculture: fertilisers → eutrophication; pesticides → resistance and biomagnification; over-irrigation → water logging and salinity.
- Alternative energy: solar, wind, hydro, biogas, geothermal, tidal.
- Land degradation includes landslides, soil erosion and desertification.
- Every individual can conserve resources through the 3 Rs and safe disposal of medicines.

# Unit 2: Ecosystems

Living things never live alone. A pond, a forest or a field is a working unit in which plants, animals and microbes depend on one another and on light, water, air and soil. This unit explains what an ecosystem is, how it is built, how energy and nutrients move through it, and the main kinds of ecosystem found on land and in water.

## 2.1 Concept of an ecosystem

An **ecosystem** is a community of living organisms interacting with one another and with their non-living surroundings in a given area, forming a self-supporting unit through which energy flows and materials cycle. The term was introduced by the British ecologist A. G. Tansley in 1935.

Key ideas:

- It has living (**biotic**) and non-living (**abiotic**) parts that act together.
- Energy enters as sunlight and flows in one direction; nutrients go round in cycles.
- It can be any size: a drop of pond water, a pond, a forest, an ocean. The whole earth is the largest ecosystem (the **ecosphere** or biosphere).
- It can be **natural** (forest, grassland, lake) or **artificial / man-made** (crop field, aquarium, garden, reservoir).

Related terms:

| Term | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Species | Group of similar organisms that can interbreed |
| Population | All members of one species in an area |
| Community | All populations of different species living together in an area |
| Habitat | The place where an organism lives |
| Niche | The role of an organism in its ecosystem: what it eats, where it lives, how it affects others |
| Biome | A large region with a typical climate and vegetation, such as a tropical rain forest or a desert |

## 2.2 Structure of an ecosystem

Structure means the parts of the ecosystem and how they are arranged.

```text
                       ECOSYSTEM
          ┌────────────────┴────────────────┐
     Abiotic parts                     Biotic parts
  ├ Inorganic: C, N, P, water,      ├ Producers (autotrophs): green plants, algae
  │  CO2, O2, minerals              ├ Consumers (heterotrophs)
  ├ Organic: proteins, fats,        │    ├ Primary: herbivores
  │  carbohydrates, humus           │    ├ Secondary: carnivores eating herbivores
  └ Climatic: light, temperature,   │    └ Tertiary: top carnivores
     rainfall, humidity, wind, pH   └ Decomposers: bacteria, fungi
```

### Abiotic components

- **Inorganic substances:** water, carbon dioxide, oxygen, nitrogen, phosphorus, calcium and other minerals.
- **Organic substances:** carbohydrates, proteins, lipids and humus from dead matter; they link the living and non-living parts.
- **Climatic (physical) factors:** sunlight, temperature, rainfall, humidity, wind, soil type and pH. They decide which organisms can live in a place.

### Biotic components

1. **Producers (autotrophs):** green plants, algae and some bacteria that make food from CO2 and water using sunlight (photosynthesis). A few bacteria make food from chemical energy (chemosynthesis).
2. **Consumers (heterotrophs, macro-consumers):**
   - Primary consumers — herbivores (deer, grasshopper, cow, zooplankton).
   - Secondary consumers — carnivores that eat herbivores (frog, small fish, fox).
   - Tertiary consumers — top carnivores (tiger, eagle, large fish).
   - Omnivores eat both plants and animals (humans, bears).
3. **Decomposers (micro-consumers, saprotrophs):** bacteria and fungi that break down dead plants and animals into simple inorganic substances, returning nutrients to the soil and water. Without them, nutrients would stay locked in dead matter.

## 2.3 Function of an ecosystem

The main functions are:

1. Energy flow through food chains and food webs.
2. Cycling of nutrients (biogeochemical cycles).
3. Production of organic matter (productivity).
4. Regulation and development of the community (ecological succession, homeostasis).

### Productivity

- **Primary productivity:** the rate at which producers make organic matter.
  - **Gross primary productivity (GPP):** total organic matter made by photosynthesis.
  - **Net primary productivity (NPP):** GPP minus what the plants use in their own respiration; this is what is available to consumers.
- **Secondary productivity:** the rate at which consumers form new tissue.

Tropical rain forests, coral reefs and estuaries are among the most productive ecosystems; deserts and the open ocean are among the least productive per unit area.

## 2.4 Energy flow

The sun is the source of energy for almost all ecosystems. Producers capture only a small part of the sunlight falling on them. At each step (trophic level), most of the energy is used for living (respiration) and lost as heat, so only a small part passes on.

**Ten per cent law** (proposed by Lindeman): on average only about 10% of the energy at one trophic level is passed on to the next.

```text
Sun → Producers → Herbivores → Carnivores → Top carnivores
       10000 J      1000 J        100 J         10 J      (example only)
         ↓            ↓             ↓             ↓
       heat         heat          heat          heat
```

Features of energy flow:

- It is **unidirectional**: energy moves from producers to consumers and never returns to the sun.
- It decreases at each level, which is why food chains are usually only 4–5 steps long.
- Nutrients, unlike energy, are recycled.

## 2.5 Food chains and food webs

A **food chain** is a sequence of organisms in which each one eats the one before it and is eaten by the next. Each step is a **trophic level**.

| Type | Starts with | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Grazing food chain** | Living green plants | Grass → grasshopper → frog → snake → eagle |
| **Detritus food chain** | Dead organic matter | Fallen leaves → earthworm → bird; dead matter → bacteria and fungi → protozoa |

Examples by ecosystem:

- Pond: Phytoplankton → zooplankton → small fish → large fish → kingfisher.
- Grassland: Grass → rabbit → fox.
- Forest: Leaves → deer → tiger.

A **food web** is a network of interconnected food chains. In nature, most animals eat more than one kind of food and are eaten by more than one predator, so food chains cross-link.

```text
A simple grassland food web (each arrow means "is eaten by"):

Grass ──► Grasshopper ──► Frog ──► Snake ──► Eagle
Grass ──► Rabbit ───────────────► Fox
Grass ──► Rabbit ─────────────────────────► Eagle
Seeds ──► Mouse ──► Snake
Seeds ──► Mouse ──► Owl
Grass ──► Grasshopper ──► Bird ──► Eagle
```

**Importance of food webs:** they make the ecosystem stable. If one prey species declines, the predator can switch to another food, so the system does not collapse.

### Biomagnification

Some pollutants that do not break down and dissolve in fat (DDT, mercury, some other pesticides) are not excreted. Their concentration increases at each step up the food chain, so top carnivores (fish-eating birds, humans) carry the highest levels. This is **biomagnification**. DDT caused thin egg shells and population decline in birds of prey.

## 2.6 Ecological pyramids

An **ecological pyramid** shows the relationship between trophic levels as a graph, with producers at the base and top carnivores at the apex.

| Pyramid | What it shows | Shape |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Pyramid of numbers** | Number of organisms at each level | Upright in grassland and pond; **spindle-shaped** in a tree food chain (one tree, many insects, fewer birds); fully **inverted** in a parasite food chain (one tree → many birds → still more parasites on them) |
| **Pyramid of biomass** | Total dry weight of living matter at each level | Upright on land; **inverted** in a pond or ocean, where a small standing mass of fast-growing phytoplankton supports a larger mass of zooplankton and fish |
| **Pyramid of energy** | Energy flowing through each level per unit time | **Always upright**, because energy is lost at every step |

```text
Upright (grassland numbers)         Spindle (tree numbers)
           ▲   hawks                        ███   birds
          ███  snakes                   ███████████ insects (many)
         █████ frogs                         █     one tree
      █████████ grasshoppers
    █████████████ grass
```

## 2.7 Biogeochemical (nutrient) cycles

Nutrients move from the environment into organisms and back again. These movements are **biogeochemical cycles**.

### Water (hydrological) cycle

Evaporation from oceans, lakes and soil + transpiration from plants → water vapour → condensation into clouds → precipitation (rain, snow) → runoff into rivers and seepage into groundwater → back to the oceans.

### Carbon cycle

```text
CO2 in air ──photosynthesis──► plants ──eaten──► animals
   ▲                              │                 │
   │ respiration, decay,          └──── death ──────┤
   │ burning of fuels                               ▼
   └──────────────── decomposers, fossil fuels ◄── dead matter
```

Burning of fossil fuels and deforestation add CO2 faster than plants and oceans remove it, which drives global warming.

### Nitrogen cycle

Air is about 78% nitrogen, but most organisms cannot use N2 directly.

| Step | What happens | Done by |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Nitrogen fixation | N2 → ammonia/nitrogen compounds | *Rhizobium* in legume root nodules, free-living bacteria (*Azotobacter*), blue-green algae, lightning, industrial fertiliser manufacture |
| Assimilation | Plants absorb nitrate and ammonium and make proteins; animals eat plants | Plants, animals |
| Ammonification | Dead matter and wastes → ammonia | Decomposer bacteria and fungi |
| Nitrification | Ammonia → nitrite → nitrate | *Nitrosomonas*, then *Nitrobacter* |
| Denitrification | Nitrate → N2 gas returned to air | Denitrifying bacteria (for example *Pseudomonas*) |

### Phosphorus cycle

A sedimentary cycle with no gaseous phase: phosphate is weathered from rocks into soil, taken up by plants, passed to animals, returned by decomposers, and partly lost to ocean sediments. Excess phosphate from fertilisers and detergents causes eutrophication.

## 2.8 Ecological succession

**Ecological succession** is the gradual, orderly replacement of one community by another in an area until a stable **climax community** is reached.

- **Primary succession** starts on bare ground where no life existed (bare rock, new sand, a new pond).
- **Secondary succession** starts where a community was removed but soil remains (abandoned farmland, burnt forest). It is faster.
- The first organisms are **pioneer species** (lichens on rock; phytoplankton in water).
- The stages in between are **seral stages**; the whole series is a **sere**.
- **Hydrosere** begins in water, **xerosere** on a dry area such as rock.

```text
Bare rock → lichens → mosses → grasses and herbs → shrubs → trees (climax forest)
```

## 2.9 Forest ecosystem

**Introduction:** land areas dominated by trees, covering a large part of the earth's land.

**Types:**

| Type | Main features | Indian examples |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Tropical rain (evergreen) forest | Heavy rainfall, warm all year, dense multi-layered canopy, very high biodiversity | Western Ghats, north-east India, Andaman and Nicobar |
| Tropical deciduous forest | Seasonal rain; trees shed leaves in the dry season | Teak and sal forests of central India |
| Tropical thorn / scrub forest | Low rainfall; thorny trees and shrubs | Parts of Rajasthan, Gujarat, Deccan |
| Temperate (coniferous) forest | Cold, snow; cone-bearing evergreen trees | Pine, fir and deodar forests of the Himalaya |
| Mangrove forest | Salt-tolerant trees on tidal coasts | Sundarbans |

**Structure:**

- Producers: trees (teak, sal, pine), shrubs, herbs, climbers.
- Primary consumers: insects, birds, deer, rabbits, elephants, squirrels.
- Secondary and tertiary consumers: snakes, foxes, wolves, tigers, leopards, hawks.
- Decomposers: fungi and bacteria in the thick leaf litter.
- Abiotic: soil, organic matter, rainfall, light, temperature.

**Function and importance:** high productivity; store carbon; regulate climate and water; protect soil; supply timber, food and many medicinal plants; home to tribal communities.

## 2.10 Grassland ecosystem

**Introduction:** areas dominated by grasses with few or no trees, where rainfall is too low for forests but more than in deserts.

**Types:** tropical grasslands (savannas, with scattered trees, as in Africa and parts of India), temperate grasslands (prairies of North America, steppes of Asia, pampas of South America), and Himalayan alpine meadows.

**Characteristic features:** moderate seasonal rainfall, grazing animals, periodic fires that keep trees out, deep fertile soil (many are now farmland).

**Structure:**

- Producers: grasses, herbs, some shrubs.
- Primary consumers: cows, buffaloes, deer, rabbits, grasshoppers, termites.
- Secondary consumers: frogs, snakes, lizards, foxes.
- Tertiary consumers: hawks, eagles, wolves.
- Decomposers: bacteria and fungi.

**Threats:** overgrazing, conversion to farmland and land degradation, which can lead to desertification.

## 2.11 Desert ecosystem

**Introduction:** regions with very low and irregular rainfall (usually under about 25 cm a year), high evaporation and sparse life.

**Types:** hot deserts (Thar in Rajasthan, Sahara) and cold deserts (Ladakh).

**Characteristic features:** very hot days and cold nights in hot deserts, sandy or rocky soil poor in organic matter, strong winds, little vegetation.

**Adaptations:**

| Plants (xerophytes) | Animals |
| --- | --- |
| Thick waxy cuticle, few or spiny leaves (cactus, opuntia, acacia) | Burrow and stay active at night |
| Fleshy stems store water | Concentrated urine, little sweating |
| Deep or widely spread roots | Camel stores fat in its hump and tolerates water loss |
| Short life cycle after rain | Thick skin, scales (reptiles) |

**Structure:** producers — cacti, shrubs, some grasses; consumers — insects, reptiles, rodents, camels, birds, foxes; decomposers — few, as heat and dryness slow decay.

## 2.12 Aquatic ecosystems

Aquatic ecosystems are **freshwater** (ponds, lakes, streams, rivers) or **marine** (oceans), with **estuaries** where the two meet.

### Pond ecosystem

A small, shallow body of still water; often seasonal.

| Component | Examples |
| --- | --- |
| Abiotic | Water, dissolved O2 and CO2, minerals, light, temperature, bottom mud |
| Producers | Phytoplankton (algae), rooted plants (*Hydrilla*), floating plants (water lettuce, duckweed) |
| Primary consumers | Zooplankton, snails, insect larvae, tadpoles |
| Secondary consumers | Small fish, frogs, water beetles |
| Tertiary consumers | Large fish, water snakes, kingfishers, herons |
| Decomposers | Bacteria and fungi in the bottom mud |

### Lake ecosystem

Larger and deeper than a pond. A lake has zones:

```text
Shore  ───────────── water surface ─────────────
  │ LITTORAL zone  │        LIMNETIC zone          (light reaches; phytoplankton, fish)
  │ (shallow,      │ ─ ─ ─ ─ light limit ─ ─ ─ ─ ─
  │ rooted plants) │        PROFUNDAL zone         (dark, cold; few organisms)
  └────────────────┴──── BENTHIC zone (bottom mud: decomposers, worms) ─────
```

Lakes are classed as **oligotrophic** (clear, nutrient-poor, rich in oxygen) or **eutrophic** (nutrient-rich, algal blooms, low oxygen in deep water). Thermal stratification develops in summer in deep lakes in temperate regions.

### Stream and river ecosystems

Flowing (lotic) water. Features: continuous flow in one direction, well-oxygenated water, organisms adapted to current (attached algae, insects with hooks, streamlined fish). A **stream** is small, fast and cool near its source; a **river** is larger, slower and warmer in the plains, carrying silt. Rivers carry nutrients and also pollutants downstream, supply water for drinking and irrigation, and form fertile plains.

### Ocean ecosystem

Oceans cover about 71% of the earth's surface. Features: salt water, great depth, tides and currents.

| Zone | Features |
| --- | --- |
| Coastal (intertidal) zone | Covered and uncovered by tides; rich in life |
| Open sea, upper lit (photic) zone | Phytoplankton make most of the ocean's food |
| Deep sea (aphotic) zone | Dark, cold, high pressure; animals feed on matter falling from above |
| Special areas | Coral reefs (very high biodiversity), mangroves |

Importance: food (fish), oxygen from phytoplankton, regulation of climate, minerals, oil and gas, and marine sources of drugs (some anticancer and antibacterial compounds come from marine organisms).

### Estuary ecosystem

An **estuary** is a partly enclosed coastal area where a river meets the sea, so fresh and salt water mix (brackish water). Examples: mouths of the Ganga (Sundarbans), Mahanadi, Godavari.

Features: changing salinity with tides, high nutrients brought by rivers, high productivity, mangroves and salt marshes, nurseries for fish and prawns. Organisms are adapted to changing salinity. Estuaries filter pollutants and protect the coast from storms, but are threatened by pollution, reclamation and over-fishing.

## Remember

- Ecosystem = biotic community + abiotic environment working as one unit (term by Tansley, 1935).
- Structure: abiotic (inorganic, organic, climatic) + biotic (producers, consumers, decomposers).
- Functions: energy flow, nutrient cycling, productivity, succession.
- Energy flow is one-way; about 10% passes to the next level (Lindeman).
- Food chains: grazing and detritus; a food web makes the system stable.
- Pyramid of energy is always upright; numbers can be spindle-shaped (tree) or inverted (parasites), biomass can be inverted (pond, ocean).
- Nitrogen cycle: fixation, assimilation, ammonification, nitrification, denitrification.
- Succession: pioneer → seral stages → climax; primary and secondary.
- Ecosystem types: forest, grassland, desert, and aquatic (pond, lake, stream, river, ocean, estuary).
- Lake zones: littoral, limnetic, profundal, benthic. Estuary = brackish, very productive.
